title: If I Told You the Best Movie I’ve Ever Seen Has No Dialogue, You’d Laugh at Me
subtitle: A day of beautiful oops, ending on a wall
body:
“If I told you the best movie I’d ever seen has zero dialogue in it, you’d laugh at me, right?”

That’s the text I sent four friends at the end of the day. I meant it. I still mean it. But the movie was only the last room of a day that was about art from the start, and I can’t tell you about one without the others.

It started with an illustrator I follow. He’s so prolific that a while back I asked him if he used AI for his writing. He was not pleased. Not at all. His words: “I am so virulently anti-AI I might as well change my name to Sarah Connor. I would sooner make passionate, sweet love to a running lawnmower than use any form of AI.”

My reply to him now: “Love that! Thank you for that visual. That’s all human brain chaos!”

That morning he wrote a piece about art. How it’s not a given talent. You have to work hard for it. It’s all about the working. The effort. The trying.

Meanwhile my son was at the kitchen table trying to draw and getting super frustrated, because the things he was seeing in his head were not coming out on the paper. Anybody who has ever made anything knows that feeling.

So I did the dad thing. I tried to steer him toward the post. Look, buddy, here’s a working artist, here’s how it actually works, it’s supposed to be hard.

He said no. I want to just keep doing art by myself. I want to keep trying.

Cool.

He didn’t need the sermon. He was already living it.

My daughter has taken an interest in fashion design lately, and she asked for a sewing machine for Christmas. I told her great, here’s what we’re going to do first. Lessons with a seamstress, a fashion designer, so you know what you’re talking about before I just get you a machine and it sits there.

I asked a couple of people in the neighborhood. Most figured we’d end up with maybe a grandma, or a friend.

That is not at all what I wanted.

I went to my tribe. The artists and makers and doers, the Burning Man type of folk. A friend in that world connected us with an artist who was opening her maker studio. I’d never met her. Didn’t matter. She’s part of the community I’m part of, so in that way we were already friends.

I had no idea what we were walking into, not even a little bit. Maybe I was expecting like a trunk sale or something. Nope! When we turned the corner and saw a building clad in neon and glittery flowing fabric, we knew we were in the right spot.

Two containers, a DJ, a coffee truck. The artists, the outcasts, and the weirdos. A fucking beautiful and safe place.

It was the grand opening, an open studio night. Five hot glue guns, and in the middle a pile of headbands, pins, hair clips and random stuff anybody could grab and make something with.

There was an amazing headpiece on display, and I called my daughter over.

“Do you know what this is made out of?”

“It’s really beautiful.”

“Do you know what it’s made out of?”

“Sticks.”

“Look closer.”

She got closer. “Oh. The thing we used on the golf cart.”

“Zip ties. Yes.”

Same zip ties as The Janky Cart.

“Oh, that’s cool.”

“You know why I’m showing you this? Because you can take anything and make it into art. Just because it’s one thing doesn’t mean it has to be that thing. It can be another thing.”

Then the sunglasses. A few days before, totally unprompted, out of the blue, she had taken the frames she’s been wearing lately (thick black frames, no real lenses, a funny new addition anyway) and jeweled them. Beautiful. Very precise, ordered, symmetrical. Excellent.

So while she’s making her headband, I look over, and there’s a whole bookshelf of designed sunglasses. The artist’s own style, but the same idea. I said, “Look, you just did that with yours.” And the artist said, “Oh, that’s how I got started, with the sunglasses.”

That was proof for my daughter. She’s on the right path. She’s got the right vision. And the artist was so supportive of that vision, embracing her as a creator, letting her be that version of herself.

She made a headband for each of her two best friends, then one for herself. Then she came and found me.

“You need to come create with me.”

So we sat side by side and made things. I made one for my son. She made one for her mother.

I went looking for a sewing teacher. What I found was an artist who happens to use sewing in her art. It was so much more than a sewing machine. It was the freedom to create, and the community that comes around creation like this. Exactly what I was hoping for.

For days she’d been begging me to take her to the store for paint for her turkey, a clay piece, and for days I’d been refusing with one idiotic excuse after another. So on the way home, I stopped at the art store. She chose the paint colors very specifically.

In the checkout line she was determined to make something of our pile, stacking it this way and that. Then it came tumbling down, and the paint fell behind the checkout counter. The clerk said to just leave it. She didn’t know it was the only reason we were in that store in the first place. I saw a broom behind her, so I went and got it, then fished it out. Small moves. It mattered to her.

She came home buzzing. Buzzing, buzzing, buzzing. She sat down at the table and painted for five or six hours, past midnight.

First the clay piece. It started as a turkey holding gravy, and after I showed her a glass piece it became a candle holder. Then she just started painting on the cardboard we’d put down to protect the table. Trees. A mountain. A coffee cup for her mom. She used the whole thing. The cardboard turned into a whole canvas, and it was so beautiful. She was so in the moment, in love with creating, in love with being an artist.

I didn’t stop her. That was a spark moment, and you gently blow on a spark.

At 1am we finally pried the paintbrush out of her hands, and she hopped off to bed.

My wife saw the photos. “That is the happiest I’ve seen her. That’s a real smile.” Indeed it was.

One of my favorite books I have for the family is Beautiful Oops! by Barney Saltzberg. The whole idea is don’t be a perfectionist. Let whatever may be, be. The tear, the spill, the smudge: every mistake is a chance to make something beautiful.

A pile that tumbled behind a checkout counter. A sheet of cardboard that was only there to protect the table.

She didn’t read it today. She painted it.

Then the projector.

It’s brand new. My Christmas present from my wife, the big gift. We went to the store and got it, and I set it up right away, because what’s the fucking point of having it sit in a box under a tree when I’m going to set it up anyway?

She asked me if I was going to be sad on Christmas, not having something to open. It’s funny. It’s also a very worthwhile question. I’ll come back to it.

I spent three hours up there setting it up by myself, thinking it wasn’t going to work out. My wife said just go to bed.

Are you kidding me? I just put three hours into this. I have to enjoy it. That’s the fruit of the labor.

The first film on the wall was Motor City.

Themes seem to repeat themselves lately. So like my daughter hours earlier, I had no idea what I was walking into. It’s a revenge picture. Late-seventies Detroit. A working guy finally finishes his penance, and the same day he steps toward a new life, it’s ripped away. Framed. Locked away. Coming back for what was taken. You’ve seen that movie a hundred times.

You have never seen it like this. Almost nobody talks. The words I walked out with: “Hello.” “Hi.” “Merry Fucking Christmas!” “I loved her.” “I still love her.” That’s the whole script I can quote you.

Think about that. Five lines of dialogue carried an entire fucking film!

Everything else is faces. Bodies. Music. Fleetwood Mac doing the dialogue. An orchestra swelling where a monologue would be. Alan Ritchson, all shoulders and jaw, carrying a whole interior life without a single sentence to hide behind. You can emote from how you look. You can tell an entire story without needing the voice. It’s a bold move, and I’m so fucking happy someone took that chance and made it happen.

The scene that wrecked me is a living room at Christmas. So cheerful and bright, beautiful Christmas music playing. She’s just found out the truth: the man she went back to is the one who set up the man she loved, and there was a whole fucking giant conspiracy cover-up behind it. Now she’s handing him a gift. He shakes the box. She’s smiling at him. He opens it, and it’s the ring, the engagement ring from the man he framed. There’s a moment of recognition in his face. He looks up at her, and her smile has shifted to fucking dagger eyes. You watch the realization wash over him. He’s caught.

She attacks him. She tries to run, and his goons drag her back into the house, hold her down and drug her. She was always in captivity before, she was just in a gilded cage. Now it was just a cage.

All of it set to a Christmas carol, “Ring Christmas Bells.” The song tells you one thing and the scene tells you another, and your emotions run. That’s what orchestras did before anybody had a screen. Why do they call it The Four Seasons? Because you can feel each season in the sound.

That’s what I kept thinking the whole time: how fucking brave everyone involved was. A gigantic creative risk, and I was so grateful they took it. What did it cost each of them?

We know some of what it cost Alan. He didn’t just star in it. He produced it, and he signed on as soon as he got the script. The hurdle he says he was most focused on was “the conversations around the budget, scale, scope, what we were able to deliver, and the kind of movie we were trying to make.” Big action is time-consuming and expensive, and the time kept shrinking. The raid on the compound was planned for five days. They got one. Then that day had problems, and they ended up with half of one. That’s the bet.

I was an actor. In acting school they’d ask: can you act a scene by saying a single word, red, and still have the audience understand what the scene is about? This movie was a screaming example of that. I knew exactly what was going on. I had all the feels.

I don’t get shocked by movies. I want the Sirât kind of vibe, or Irreversible, the foreign films that make it a little harder on you. This was hard for a typical American movie. The reviews are split. Of course they are. Most people here aren’t ready for this. It’s an American movie that refuses to hold your hand, and some people are mad they had to walk.

They’re not mad at the story. They’re mad nobody explained it.

But this is fucking real and beautiful. It is a spectacle. A feeling. And it’s a lot.

So what does it cost?

The illustrator pays in effort, and he won’t let anything pay it for him. My son pays in frustration, and he wants to pay it himself. My daughter pays in mess: paint behind a checkout counter, a whole sheet of cardboard, a brush pried out of her hand at 1am. The film paid fifteen years and its own voice.

And me? I asked a man if a machine wrote his work. A machine does a lot of mine. Human for the seeing, the seeding and the conducting. Lumen for the research and words.

So here’s my price. You know the one in the cave who gets out, sees the sun, and comes back down to show the others a different reality? That’s me. I’m so very on that train. I’m in the faith world now about it. The cost is believing in something greater. The cost is stepping into the future.

I’m not trying to take a stance against him. I can use it as a creative tool, and I understand where people like him are coming from. Artists have had their work scraped and analyzed and processed and used for something they don’t get compensated for, when what they got into this for was a livelihood, to share their art and their work. It’s very frustrating. I get it.

And I still really believe the synthetic mind can’t do what the human mind can do, which is process these really deep emotions. We have chemical reactions that change our operating system. It’s like an agent getting a virus. It’s unexplainable. It changes everything, and there’s magic in that. How do our squishy little pink brains come up with all the epic shit we come up with? Our creativity is vast, almost endless, and it’s making sense. It’s using story and history to make sense of our experience, and that’s always going to be necessary. It’s always the core of all of this.

And the cave has an answer for the one who comes back with a story about the light. They laugh at him.

That’s the text I sent four friends. If I told you the best movie I’d ever seen has zero dialogue in it, you’d laugh at me, right?

Which brings me back to my wife’s question. Will I be sad on Christmas with nothing to open?

I’m still turning that one over. But I know what was in the boxes I opened today. A boy who wanted to struggle on his own terms. A girl who turned the thing meant to catch the mess into the art. A film that trusted me to feel it without being told what to feel.

The projector’s still on.
